text.p: The managing director of Australian nickel producer QNI Ltd on Friday defended his company's planned merger with South Africa-based miner Gencor Ltd's nickel business against growing criticism that the A$2.3 billion deal shortchanges shareholders.
"We're acquiring assets that give the company a greater strength both in size and in quality of our assets, and it does it immediately," Wyn Davies told Reuters in an interview.
QNI shares have traded lower since the deal was announced this week after analysts said shareholders wouldn't like it.
Then brokers Prudential Bache and Wilson HTM downgraded QNI to "sell" and speculation flew that the deal would not pass shareholders at an extraordinary meeting yet to be convened.
Under the merger, Gencor gets a 56 percent stake in QNI through the issue of 524.8 million new shares. In return Gencor rolls its nickel assets into QNI.
In late Friday trading QNI was nine cents down at A$2.56 after losing three cents the previous day -- a far cry from the A$3.40 to A$3.50 some brokers were touting the stock would fetch on Thursday.
Investors may have unduly caught the jitters, because of the international flavour of the deal, Davies suggested.
Gencor is based in Johannesburg but its main nickel asset is its Cerro Matoso mine and smelter in Colombia.
Gencor and QNI already share mining activities in Indonesia and QNI has long purchased ore from New Caledonia.
But QNI has always hauled everything back to Australia for processing at its Yabulu refinery in Queensland.
"In Australia everyone is concerned when you're becoming an international company or have a relationship with an international company, everyone gets worried about selling off the farm," Davies said.
He said the merged entity would be based in Queensland and retain its Australian Stock Exchange listing.
But structural changes afoot in the nickel industry, brought on by new low cost production leaves little room for companies hobbled by limited markets and inflated costs, he said.
In a few years, the massive Voisey's Bay nickel mine in Labrador, Canada, would be in full swing, dramatically reducing the benchmark by which industry mining costs are measured.
More low cost production is planned in Indonesia and Western Australia. Closer to home, a second nickel refinery in Queensland has been proposed by potential rival Calliope Metals Corp

"You have to take cognisance of the changes and the structure of the market," Davies said. By merging QNI with the Gencor assets, shareholders get a leg up on other nickel companies that may face cost pressures, he said.
"It puts us in a much more competitive position, and we're doing it before Voisey's Bay comes on," he said.

A main criticism of the QNI/Gencor deal, which needs QNI shareholder and government approvals, is that it would dilute earnings per share (EPS) by 20 percent in the first year and would remain dilutive in the second before turning positive.
Davies said the dilution was related to capital investments, that naturally brought with it "a little bit of pain to begin with" before a rapid upturn on the positive side.
A positive impact on earnings would be directly linked to international nickel prices at the time, he said.
The cyclical nature of nickel puts added emphasis on costs and in that area, Gencor's Cerro Matoso has the clear advantage.

Davies estimated the cost of producing nickel in Queensland is above US$2.14 a pound, while in Colombia it is "well below US$2.00." Nickel curently fetches about US$3.33 cents a pound, depending on grade.
"It's a manageable price at the moment," Davies said.
Yabulu produced 27,000 tonnes of nickel last year and Cerro Matoso 24,000 tonnes, although both are capable of churning out closer to 30,000 tonnes each at full capacity.
A merger would create one of the world's top five nickel groups, accounting for about eight percent of the world market.
Plans to boost ferronickel (high iron-bearing) production at Cerro Matoso a further 20,000 tonnes at some point, would provide an even stronger global presence, he said.
